When a Formal Logarithm Fails

Corrections, cohomology, and a spectral sequence in characteristic three

Henry Shin · October 2026

PDF · 12 pagesMarkdown manuscriptTeX source

Begin with formal power series and linear algebra over a field. Cochain complexes, filtrations and the required spectral sequence are constructed in the text; the final interpretation uses exact triangles.

The identity changes multiplication into addition. Near , it becomes a formal power-series identity: no convergence or choice of branch is involved. In characteristic three, its first two orders can still be recovered. The next order cannot.

We will follow that failure through a single calculation. Substitution becomes a coproduct, an attempted identity becomes a cocycle condition, and a correction removes a boundary. The first residual that cannot be removed is detected by a nonzero differential in a spectral sequence. Its polynomial then supplies the addition law of a different group, where the same compatibility equation proves associativity.

The opening requires formal power series and arithmetic in characteristic three. Tensor products and cochain complexes are introduced as they become useful. Sections 5–6 give the complete spectral-sequence calculation; section 7 interprets it through a tower of exact triangles. The argument uses only finitely many polynomial weights, so no convergence theorem for an infinite spectral sequence is needed.

Let be a field. Write a unit near as . Multiplication gives the law

In characteristic , , and that inference loses information. There is a second issue: a logarithm with the required normalization does not exist. The coefficients with denominator divisible by signal an actual obstruction, not merely a poor formula.

For characteristic three, the obstruction has a short proof. The threefold sum under is

The threefold sum under the additive law is zero. Consequently any formal-group homomorphism from the multiplicative group to the additive group satisfies

Substitution is injective on , so . In particular, there is no such homomorphism with linear coefficient .

This proves nonexistence. The question that remains is more precise: how far can the desired identity be constructed, and which part of its failure cannot be changed by another coefficient? From now on, .

The Frobenius calculation in What a Derivative Retains explains this distinction; Divisibility of Separated Polynomials uses these coefficients to retain multiplicities in a fiber.

The diagonal gives a geometric setting for these coefficients. Put . The completed tensor product is

Our identity asks for another compatibility as well: the coefficients must respect a group law. That law pulls functions in the other direction:

Thus the diagonal identifies two points, while evaluates a function on their group product. In tensor notation,

For , this is the simple identity

An element with constant term one satisfying this identity is called group-like. An element satisfying

Associativity now has a reusable algebraic form:

Both sides send to . This coassociativity will ensure that failures of the primitive equation satisfy a compatibility equation of their own.

The same multiplicative law already occurs in the line-bundle calculation in What a Derivative Retains. In Fourier, Symmetry, and Reconstruction, §12.4, a logarithmic coordinate makes tensor products of unipotent monodromies additive over . Our calculation examines the obstruction to that universal coordinate change in characteristic three. It does not prohibit every logarithm calculation in a sufficiently small nilpotent quotient.

The part of the coproduct that preserves weight is

Here is the additive cobar differential. This decomposition uses the chosen coordinate and its homogeneous monomials; the filtration itself is the sequence of order cutoffs just defined.

Three gradings or indices now have separate roles. Cohomological degree counts input slots. Weight counts powers of the formal coordinates. The index of a spectral-sequence differential will measure how far the first remaining defect raises weight.

Only weights at most four are needed below. We may therefore do the entire calculation in the finite complex . It is finite-dimensional: a nonzero normalized tensor of weight below five has at most four slots. This quotient truncates the whole complex by total weight. It is not asserted to be the cobar complex of ; that ideal need not define a quotient compatible with the coproduct.

7 · The tower behind the pages

Let . Successive truncations fit into short exact sequences of complexes

They give exact triangles in the derived category of -vector spaces,

and connecting maps

To compute , choose a representative lift to and apply . Its differential lies in the kernel, which is the new weight layer. Another lift differs by a cochain in that layer, so its differential changes by a -boundary. This proves that the obstruction class is independent of the chosen lift. Its vanishing is equivalent to the existence of a correction making the lift a cocycle.

Our calculation follows two consecutive stages:

Partial solution Next residual Obstruction class Result
in Zero in Correct by and lift to
in Nonzero in No lift to

The spectral sequence organizes such successive lift-and-correct calculations, accounting for the ambiguity in earlier choices. In this example the quadratic correction is unique, and the second obstruction is the nonzero just computed. The weight-four calculation verifies that its value is defined on the second page.

There is a direct comparison with the edge-removal obstruction in What a Boundary Map Can Prove. There a connecting map measures whether local data extend across an edge. Here successive connecting maps measure whether an identity extends by one polynomial order. The complexes differ, but the operation is the same: lift a representative, take its differential, and identify the resulting class modulo changes of lift.

Formal-group obstruction calculations have long used degree filtrations in this way. Rezk's account of the Lubin–Tate theorem constructs a complex of symmetric cocycles, filters by polynomial degree, and calculates the resulting spectral sequence. His two-term symmetric-cocycle complex differs from the full normalized cobar complex used here; it provides a close setting for the method and its wider role.3

8 · The obstruction becomes an addition law

The same cubic class has a constructive use. Its additive cocycle identity is

The two bracketings of a threefold sum have equal first coordinates. Their second coordinates differ by the two sides of the cocycle identity. They are therefore equal. Symmetry of proves commutativity, gives the identity , and gives inverse .

This is the addition law of length-two, -typical Witt vectors over . To see the coefficient directly, first work over the integers with the two ghost polynomials

Requiring both ghost coordinates to add forces the second coordinate of a sum to be

The quotient is an integer polynomial. Reducing it modulo three gives the displayed addition law; no division by three is performed in .4

The extension retains information absent from the two separate additive coordinates. Its threefold sum is

Indeed, and , so the second coordinate of three copies is . Componentwise addition on would have zero three-series. The cubic correction changes the group structure even though the underlying space remains the affine plane.

The projection is a homomorphism to , with kernel the additive second coordinate. Thus supplies the data of an extension. This construction gives a different group law; it does not produce the scalar logarithm ruled out in section 1. A polynomial that obstructed one compatibility problem now enforces associativity in another.

9 · What the filtered object retains

The additive and multiplicative formal groups both have underlying formal disk . Their continuous cotangent modules are both , and their tangent spaces at the identity are one-dimensional. That information cannot decide whether a normalized logarithm exists. The difference lies in how two formal points are combined.

Keeping the coproduct retains that combination. Passing to the associated graded makes its lowest-order law additive. Keeping the filtered complex as well retains the interaction between successive orders. Its differential records the original identity, its boundaries record available corrections, and its later spectral-sequence differentials record failures that remain after earlier corrections have been made.

In the derived category, the exact triangles specify the obstruction targets and prove independence from choices. The finite tower may equivalently be regarded as a tower of -module spectra, where its connecting maps become connecting maps of spectra. That reformulation does not introduce additional information into this calculation. Further spectral questions require further structured input; the completed Hopf algebra has supplied the nonlinear law throughout.

The distinction also explains why the two remedies for a vanishing derivative have different jobs. Higher Taylor coefficients recover variation that first order cannot see. Cohomology determines whether those coefficients can be chosen compatibly with a specified law. Better coefficient detection cannot make an impossible logarithm exist. It can expose its obstruction, locate the first order where it appears, and show how that same obstruction participates in another construction.
